question: What happened to the people who carry words between languages when machines were promised to replace them in 1954, and what does that say about which part of translation work stays with people today?

issues.note: The narration 'that is translation: the written word' plays over a remote video-interpreting room (an interpreter on a call). The picture shows spoken or sign interpreting while the words describe written translation, so picture and narration disagree.

The title-card question about 'the people who carry words between languages' stays on the translator desk, then hard-cuts to the library exterior mid-sentence. The question sits on a picture that has no obvious link to the following street scene.
R13.2 to R13.5 (about 16 s) hold the same wide shot of the video-call booth with the same blue wall and almost no movement while the narration covers remote and sign-language interpreting.
R13.6 to R13.8 (about 12 s) hold the same close-up of the signing figure on the screen, with only text overlays changing.
R12.6 and R12.7 repeat the same static wide shot of the lone worker at a desk (also seen in R11) while statistics narration runs. Little that is new to look at.
From R17.2 to R17.7 (about 24 s) the dusk street slowly dollies with almost no new information after the closing line, so the ending lingers.
